Analytic parametrices and straight characteristics

*Written by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Public domain (CC0). *

A directional inverse can carry a singularity forward or backward along a characteristic line. To use that inverse at analytic regularity, its error must itself be analytic. We construct two such inverses for constant-coefficient equations, prove their analytic wavefront bounds, and then propagate singularities at every derivative-growth scale. The spatial cutoff in the propagation argument is smooth; we keep track of the analytic directions it introduces. An imaginary displacement estimate quantifies the error for every further real perturbation vector.

Use , the Fourier inverse factor , and complex-linear distribution pairings. Let and let be a polynomial of degree . Its top homogeneous part is denoted by . Here real principal type means The lower coefficients may be complex. Euler's identity , obtained by differentiating at , shows that at every real , including noncharacteristic points.

The available proofs used below are holomorphic boundary directions, Theorem 2; conic decomposition, Theorem 4; analytic pullback, Theorem 2; convolution directions, Corollary 7; and analytic differential regularity, Theorem 3. Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts, Theorems 5–7, supplies projection, comparison, multiplication and differentiation. Convolution as addition of supports, B0–B3 and Theorem 1.1, supplies distributional pairings and derivative commutation. Holomorphic boundaries in convex cones supplies the polydisk proof turning coordinate holomorphy into power series. The supplied Fourier, integration, finite-algebra and metric/calculus readings justify the inversions, finite-order pairings, determinants, compactness and cutoffs used here.

Proof. The first two assertions are that theorem, for any finite closed conic cover. The present proof is an additional consequence of propagation and does not replace that more general result.

Proof locations and mathematical source

  • Holomorphic boundaries and analytic directions, Theorem 2, supplies the full-cone boundary estimate used in (19). The growth bound here is uniform even near the cone's edge.

  • Boundary regularity and conic decomposition, Theorem 4, supplies the actual direction-selecting operators. Lemma 4 above proves their required commutation. Analytic pullback and cotangent directions, Theorem 2, controls the spatial cutoff, and Keeping zero covectors in kernel operations, Corollary 7, supplies the exact convolution bound.

  • Both analytic directions at support boundaries and Analytic equations and characteristic directions supply the closed support-normal inclusion and noncharacteristic differential regularity. Characteristic planes and convex-domain uniqueness, Corollary 5, retains the more general compact-support alternative mentioned in Exercise 8.

  • Lars Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I, second edition, 2003 reprint, Definition 8.3.5, Lemma 8.3.6 and Theorem 8.3.7, pp. 275–278, and Theorems 8.6.12–8.6.13 with Corollary 8.6.14, pp. 313–315, are the mathematical antecedents. The weighted graph homotopy, exposition, exercises and figure here are independently expressed. The general smooth Fourier-integral propagation theorem has its separate programme proof; it is not being used as an analytic estimate.

  • Lars Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I: Distribution Theory and Fourier Analysis, second-edition reprint, Springer, 2003, doi:10.1007/978-3-642-61497-2, Lemma 8.3.6 for arbitrary imaginary perturbations. Lemma 2a proves the estimate in every positive degree; Exercises 9–11 treat zeros, explicit nonlinear constants and uniform conic perturbations.
